title: Government Weighs Cutting Stakes in Four PSU Banks to 75% After IDBI Sale
excerpt: Central Bank of India, UCO Bank, Punjab & Sind Bank and Indian Overseas Bank could see government holdings cut to 75% within a year to meet SEBI public shareholding norms, The Economic Times reported.
body:
• The government is considering cutting its stake in Central Bank of India, UCO Bank, Punjab & Sind Bank and Indian Overseas Bank to 75% within about a year, The Economic Times reported.
  • The aim is regulatory, not privatisation: meeting SEBI's 25% minimum public shareholding norm. Sales would likely use the offer-for-sale route, depending on market conditions.
  • The cuts required differ sharply: Punjab & Sind Bank is at 93.85% government holding, Indian Overseas Bank 92.44%, UCO Bank 90.95% and Central Bank of India 81.19%.
  • For investors: no sale dates or sizes have been announced — watch for DIPAM and exchange filings before treating the reported plan as a confirmed transaction.

The government is considering reducing its shareholding in four public sector banks to 75% over roughly the next year, according to a report in The Economic Times, in a move aimed at meeting minimum public shareholding norms rather than transferring control of the lenders.

The four banks are Central Bank of India, UCO Bank, Punjab & Sind Bank and Indian Overseas Bank. The report, carried by Mint and other outlets on October 23, said increasing public shareholding in these banks is the immediate priority.

How big a sale each bank would need

The starting points are far above the target. The government holds 93.85% of Punjab & Sind Bank, 92.44% of Indian Overseas Bank, 90.95% of UCO Bank and 81.19% of Central Bank of India, according to the figures reported by The Economic Times and reproduced in follow-on coverage. Reaching 75% would therefore require a reduction of about 18.85 percentage points in Punjab & Sind Bank, 17.44 points in Indian Overseas Bank, 15.95 points in UCO Bank and 6.19 points in Central Bank of India.

Officials cited in the report said the government stake would likely be sold through the offer-for-sale (OFS) route, depending on market conditions, while the banks themselves could also raise capital from the market based on their own requirements and strategies. A larger public float is expected to support the banks' valuations, the report said. No timetable, sale size or pricing has been announced.

Why 75% is the line

The target follows the Securities and Exchange Board of India's minimum public shareholding requirement, under which listed companies must maintain at least 25% public ownership. State-owned companies, including financial institutions, had been exempted from that requirement until August 2026, and a further extension is expected to be notified, The Economic Times reported. Even with an extension, bringing the four banks to 75% government holding would align them with the norm.

The distinction matters for how investors should read the plan. A cut to 75% leaves the government as the clear majority owner. It is separate from privatisation, which involves transferring control to a private owner.

The IDBI backdrop

The report follows the government's announcement earlier in October that Fairfax Financial Holdings, promoted by Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa, would acquire a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for Rs 52,878 crore. That transaction, approved by the Cabinet on October 14, involves the sale of the government's 30.48% stake and LIC's 30.24% stake, leaving the government and LIC with a combined 34%.

Bank unions have opposed the IDBI sale, and the Finance Ministry has separately clarified that there is no legal bar under the IDBI (Repeal) Act, 2003 to reducing the government's stake. The four-bank plan, by contrast, does not involve a strategic buyer or a change of control.

Consolidation is the longer question

Alongside the shareholding plan, the government is preparing a strategy for the next round of public sector bank consolidation, with a long-term objective of three or four large state-owned banks, according to the report. NITI Aayog had previously shortlisted Central Bank of India and Indian Overseas Bank as potential privatisation candidates, but no final decision has been taken.

Any privatisation would require legislative changes, including amendments to the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, and those amendments could be pursued alongside the consolidation exercise, officials cited in the report said. The consolidation assessment is expected to weigh technological compatibility, geographical reach and business mix, with banks invited to offer suggestions.

What to watch

The reported plan remains under consideration. Investors should look for formal announcements from the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management, exchange disclosures from the four banks on shareholding and capital plans, and any SEBI or government notification on the public shareholding exemption. Until those appear, the 75% target is a reported intention, not a launched sale.
